meta.unit: Malachi given to the record (3 Nephi 24–25)
principles: A prophet's words delivered to people who never had them
A God who asks to be tested
Complaint quoted back to the ones who made it

world_behind.title: They did not have this text
world_behind.text: 3 Nephi 26:2 says these scriptures were ones they had not with them, and that the Father commanded they be given. 1 Nephi 5:13 has the brass plates carrying the prophets down to Jeremiah, which is where the shelf stops. Malachi wrote after Lehi had left Jerusalem, so the record explains its own gap.

world_behind.title: The frame sits inside verse 1
world_behind.text: The first sentences are narrative and the quotation begins at "Behold, I will send my messenger." 3 Nephi 25 continues the same Malachi passage without a break, so one quotation runs across two chapter numbers.

world_behind.title: The text is Malachi 3 nearly whole
world_behind.text: All eighteen verses correspond to the eighteen of Malachi 3, and eight of them differ from the King James wording in a way that is more than spelling. 3 Nephi 25 is closer still, with one of its six verses altered.

world_behind.title: Three of the differences change sense
world_behind.text: Malachi 3:5 has those that turn aside the stranger "from his right" and verse 5 here drops the phrase; Malachi 3:13 asks what have we spoken "so much" against thee and verse 13 drops it; Malachi 3:14 has kept his "ordinance" where verse 14 has ordinances. Everything else that moves is a pronoun or a connective.

world_behind.title: Malachi appears only in these two chapters
world_behind.text: No other chapter of the volume quotes him, and Isaiah is quoted in more than twenty. A prophet the Nephites had never read arrives once, in full, and is never used again.

world_behind.title: The disputational shape is Malachi's own
world_behind.text: Verses 7, 8, 13, and 14 each set up a complaint with "ye say" before answering it, and Malachi 3 does the same at the same points. The form was in the source before the Nephite editor touched it.

words.text: One sent with a message. The record uses the word twice, both in this verse, and the King James Bible thirty-four times. Verse 1 uses it of the one who prepares and of the Lord of the covenant.
One who purifies metal by heat. Treated at Alma 34:29. It appears twice, both in this chapter, in the record, and the King James Bible twice, both in Malachi 3. Verse 2 pairs it with fuller's soap.
Practitioners of magic. The record uses the word once, here, and the King James Bible six times. Verse 5 heads a list of five kinds of wrongdoing.
What is presented at the altar. The word turns up six times here, and the King James Bible two hundred and sixty-five. Verse 8 pairs it with tithes as the two things withheld.
A building where provisions are kept. One use here against two in the King James Bible. Verse 10 makes it the place the tithes go.
Something that consumes. Its count is once, here, in this book, while the King James Bible once, at Malachi 3:11. Verse 11 has it rebuked for the sake of the fields.
Precious stones, and by extension what is treasured. The record uses the word twice and the King James Bible twenty-five. Verse 17 says he will make up his jewels in that day.

phrases.term: The words which the Father had given unto Malachi
phrases.text: The attribution set out before the quotation begins. The source is named twice in the same verse.

phrases.term: After they were written he expounded them
phrases.text: The order of operations. The writing comes first and the explanation follows.

phrases.term: He is like a refiner's fire, and like fuller's soap
phrases.text: Two images of cleaning, one by heat and one by washing. Verse 3 stays with the metal and drops the soap.

phrases.term: He shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver
phrases.text: The refiner is seated. The image is of someone who stays at the work until it is done.

phrases.term: I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers
phrases.text: God as witness rather than only judge. The list names five offenses and ends with those who do not fear him.

phrases.term: Return unto me, and I will return unto you
phrases.text: The offer stated as a matched pair. Their reply in the same verse is a question about how to return.

phrases.term: Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me
phrases.text: A question answered before it can be considered. Verse 8 names tithes and offerings as the theft.

phrases.term: Prove me now herewith, saith the Lord of Hosts
phrases.text: An invitation to test him. Verse 10 attaches a specific promise to the test.

phrases.term: Your words have been stout against me
phrases.text: The complaint characterized before it is quoted. Verse 14 gives the words themselves.

phrases.term: It is vain to serve God
phrases.text: The objection stated flatly. Verse 15 extends it: the proud are happy and those who tempt God are delivered.

phrases.term: A book of remembrance was written before him
phrases.text: A record kept of a conversation. The people who feared the Lord spoke to each other, and that is what is written down.

verses.label: v. 1–18
verses.title: A light revision with one heavy exception
verses.text: Eight of this chapter's eighteen verses carry a real word change against the King James text, forty-four per cent, which places it twentieth among the twenty-four chapter-length quotations in the volume. Ten word-level edits produce that figure, and nine of them are single words. The tenth is the sixty-two word frame at the head of verse 1. Take that frame away and this is the most lightly handled prophetic chapter in the volume after 3 Nephi 25 and 2 Nephi 22.

verses.label: v. 1
verses.title: Written first, expounded after
verses.text: Malachi 3:1 begins on "Behold, I will send my messenger." Before that, this chapter supplies a scene: "he commanded them that they should write the words which the Father had given unto Malachi... And it came to pass that after they were written he expounded them." Two things follow from it that the King James text cannot say. The words are dictated for the record before they are explained, so the writing is the point of the episode. And the attribution moves: what Malachi received came from the Father, and the formula is "Thus said the Father unto Malachi." No other quoted block in the volume is introduced by an order to write it down.

verses.label: v. 5
verses.title: A stranger with no rights named
verses.text: The King James list of five offences ends with those "that turn aside the stranger from his right." Three words are deleted here and the offence is simply to "turn aside the stranger." It is the only deletion in a list otherwise reproduced exactly, and it changes what the swift witness is testifying to. In Malachi the wrong is denying a stranger a legal claim he holds. Here it is turning him away.

verses.label: v. 11
verses.title: The fields, plural
verses.text: One letter changes in the promise about the vine: the King James keeps the fruit from being cast "before the time in the field" and this reads "in the fields." Nothing else in verses 10 through 12, the tithing passage that is the best known part of the chapter, is altered at all. The windows of heaven, the devourer, the delightsome land and the proving are all reproduced word for word.

verses.label: v. 14
verses.title: Two changes in one complaint
verses.text: The people's grievance is rewritten twice over in a single verse. "What profit is it that we have kept his ordinance" becomes "what doth it profit," turning a noun phrase into a working verb, and the singular ordinance becomes ordinances, matching the plural the King James itself uses seven verses earlier at verse 7. The verse is brought into agreement with its own chapter.

verses.label: v. 16
verses.title: What the Lord heard
verses.text: The King James gives the hearing an object: "and the Lord hearkened, and heard it." The pronoun is deleted here, leaving "the Lord hearkened and heard." Nothing tells the reader what was heard, and the sentence runs straight on to the book of remembrance being written. It is the smallest edit in the chapter and it removes the one word that limited the hearing to the conversation just described.

chapter.title: The chapter explains why it exists
chapter.text: Verse 1 says these are words the Father gave Malachi, delivered here because this people did not have them. The introduction is part of the verse.

chapter.title: Writing precedes understanding
chapter.text: Verse 1 puts the explaining after the writing. The record is secured before it is interpreted.

chapter.title: The cleaning images are domestic and industrial
chapter.text: Verse 2 puts fuller's soap beside a refiner's fire. Both are ordinary trades in the ancient world.

chapter.title: The refiner sits down
chapter.text: Verse 3 gives the posture. Purifying silver is described as patient work rather than a single act.

chapter.title: Injustice and irreligion are listed together
chapter.text: Verse 5 puts withheld wages and mistreated widows beside sorcery and false swearing. The offenses are not sorted into sacred and social.

chapter.title: God asks to be tested
chapter.text: Verse 10 invites the proof. The chapter makes an experiment part of the covenant.

chapter.title: The complaints are quoted, not paraphrased
chapter.text: Verses 7, 8, 13, and 14 give the objections in the objectors' own words. The argument runs by letting them speak.

chapter.title: The last image is a conversation written down
chapter.text: Verse 16 has people talking to each other and a book kept of it. What God preserves in this chapter is what the faithful said among themselves.

applications.title: Write it before you explain it
applications.text: The words were recorded and then expounded. Getting the text down protects it from your own commentary.

applications.title: Expect the cleaning to take time
applications.text: The refiner sits. Being purified is described here as a process someone stays with.

applications.title: Pay what you owe people and what you owe God
applications.text: The chapter lists withheld wages beside withheld tithes. Both are named as theft.

applications.title: Constancy is given as the reason anything survives
applications.text: The verse ties "I am the Lord, I change not" directly to the sons of Jacob not being consumed. What has held things together is described as steadiness rather than leniency.

applications.title: Expect the honest question back
applications.text: After "return unto me and I will return unto you" the text keeps the reply: wherein shall we return? An answer is worth more when a real question is standing in front of it.

applications.title: Take the test as offered
applications.text: He asks to be proved in this one thing. An invitation to test a promise is worth accepting on its own terms.

applications.title: Notice when the wicked look happy
applications.text: Their complaint was that the proud are called happy and those who work wickedness are set up. The chapter does not deny the observation; it sets it in a longer frame.

applications.title: Talk to each other about it
applications.text: Those who feared the Lord spake often one to another, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them. The answer modeled here to a discouraging stretch is company and a written record.

questions.text: What in me would not survive a refiner's fire?
Whose wages or whose need have I turned aside?
What would returning actually look like this week?
What am I withholding and calling something else?
Have I ever tested a promise instead of debating it?
When have I said serving God was not worth it?
Who do I speak with often about him?
